qualitativeClaims.claim: Wave motion transfers energy without transferring matter.

qualitativeClaims.claim: The two main types of wave motion are transverse and longitudinal.
qualitativeClaims.expected: In transverse waves, oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; in longitudinal waves, oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Examples of transverse waves include light waves, water ripples, and waves on a rope.
qualitativeClaims.expected: These waves have crests and troughs.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Examples of longitudinal waves include sound waves and compression waves in a slinky spring.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Key wave terms are amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, and wave speed.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Amplitude is maximum displacement from rest position; wavelength is distance between consecutive corresponding points; frequency is number of waves per second; period is time for one complete oscillation; wave speed is distance travelled by the wave per second.

qualitativeClaims.claim: The wave equation links speed, frequency, and wavelength.
qualitativeClaims.expected: v = fλ, where v is wave speed in m/s, f is frequency in Hz, and λ is wavelength in m.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Frequency and period are reciprocals.
qualitativeClaims.expected: f = 1/T and T = 1/f, where T is the period in seconds.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Waves can be reflected, refracted, and diffracted.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Reflection is bouncing off a surface; refraction is bending due to change in speed; diffraction is spreading around obstacles or through gaps.

source.question: For IGCSE physics, give an overview of the types of wave motion, how waves are described, and the wave equation.

annotations.text: Transverse wave: oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, forming crests and troughs (for example light, water ripples, waves on a rope).
Longitudinal wave: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions (for example sound, a slinky spring).
Amplitude A is the maximum displacement from the rest position; wavelength λ is the distance between consecutive corresponding points.
Wave motion transfers energy without transferring matter; the wave equation is v = fλ, with frequency f in Hz, period T = 1/f, and wave speed v in m/s.

source.question: Explain the photoelectric effect (threshold frequency, work function) and the wavelength of a photon.

annotations.text: Energy balance for photoemission: a photon of energy hf strikes the metal; φ is the work function, the minimum energy needed to liberate an electron. The threshold frequency is f0 = φ/h. Any excess appears as kinetic energy K = hf − φ, so emission requires f ≥ f0. The photon wavelength follows from λ = c/f, and at threshold λ0 = c/f0 is the longest wavelength that can eject an electron.

turnPlan.question: Explain the hydraulic press using Pascal's law, with a diagram and a simple explanation.
assumptions: Liquid is incompressible and enclosed
Friction and weight of pistons are neglected (ideal press)
Both pistons are at the same height so no hydrostatic height correction

qualitativeClaims.claim: Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions throughout the fluid.
qualitativeClaims.expected: P = F/A is the same at every point in the confined liquid, so pressure under the small piston equals pressure under the large piston.

qualitativeClaims.claim: A hydraulic press has two connected cylinders of different cross-sectional areas filled with liquid, each fitted with a piston.
qualitativeClaims.expected: A small force F1 on the small piston (area A1) creates pressure P = F1/A1; this same pressure acts on the large piston (area A2), giving output force F2 = P*A2 = F1*(A2/A1).

qualitativeClaims.claim: Because A2 > A1, the output force F2 is greater than the applied force F1; the press is a force multiplier.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Mechanical advantage = F2/F1 = A2/A1 > 1.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Energy is conserved: the small piston moves through a much larger distance than the large piston rises.
qualitativeClaims.expected: F1*d1 = F2*d2 (ideal, no friction), so d2 = d1*(A1/A2); force is gained at the cost of distance.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Diagram should show two connected cylinders (narrow on left, wide on right), liquid inside, a small downward force on the small piston and a large upward force lifting a load on the large piston, with labels F1, A1, F2, A2 and equal-pressure arrows in the fluid.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Annotated sketch: small piston pushed down, pressure transmitted through liquid, large piston pushed up with load.

rows.question: Derive the range of a projectile launched on level ground, and show why 45° gives the largest range.

turnPlan.subject: physics
turnPlan.question: Derive the range of a projectile launched on level ground, and show why 45° gives the largest range.
assumptions: Level ground: launch and landing at same height
Uniform gravitational field g acting vertically downward
No air resistance
Initial speed u and launch angle θ are the only parameters; u, g fixed when maximising over θ
A verified illustration is required by the question's spatial or explicit visual request.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Resolve initial velocity u at angle θ into components: ux = u cosθ (constant), uy = u sinθ (decelerated by g).
qualitativeClaims.expected: ux = u cosθ; uy = u sinθ

qualitativeClaims.claim: Time of flight from vertical motion: y = u sinθ·t − ½gt² = 0 gives t = 0 (launch) or t = 2u sinθ/g (landing).
qualitativeClaims.expected: T = 2u sinθ / g

qualitativeClaims.claim: Range is horizontal speed times flight time: R = u cosθ · 2u sinθ/g.
qualitativeClaims.expected: R = (2u² sinθ cosθ)/g

qualitativeClaims.claim: Apply the double-angle identity 2 sinθ cosθ = sin 2θ to obtain the standard range formula.
qualitativeClaims.expected: R = u² sin(2θ) / g

qualitativeClaims.claim: For fixed u and g, R is maximised when sin(2θ) is maximised; sin(2θ) ≤ 1 with equality when 2θ = 90°.
Maximum range value at θ = 45°: R_max = u²/g.
qualitativeClaims.expected: R_max = u²/g

qualitativeClaims.claim: Calculus check: dR/dθ = (2u²/g)cos(2θ) = 0 gives θ = 45°, and d²R/dθ² = −(4u²/g)sin(2θ) < 0 there, confirming a maximum.
qualitativeClaims.expected: dR/dθ = 0 at θ = 45°; second derivative negative

turnPlan.subject: physics
turnPlan.question: Explain what an intrinsic semiconductor is.
assumptions: Standard band theory model applies
Material is a crystalline Group IV element (Si or Ge)
No external fields or impurities present
Thermal equilibrium conditions

qualitativeClaims.claim: An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor material (e.g., silicon or germanium) without any significant doping impurities.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Pure Si or Ge crystal with no added pentavalent or trivalent impurities.

qualitativeClaims.claim: At absolute zero (0 K), intrinsic semiconductors behave as perfect insulators because the valence band is completely full and the conduction band is completely empty.
qualitativeClaims.expected: No free charge carriers available for conduction at 0 K.

qualitativeClaims.claim: At room temperature, thermal energy excites some electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, creating electron-hole pairs.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Each electron that jumps to the conduction band leaves behind a hole in the valence band.

qualitativeClaims.claim: In an intrinsic semiconductor, the number of free electrons in the conduction band equals the number of holes in the valence band (n = p = ni).
qualitativeClaims.expected: Electron concentration equals hole concentration, both equal to the intrinsic carrier concentration ni.

qualitativeClaims.claim: The band gap of an intrinsic semiconductor is small (~1 eV); for silicon it is about 1.1 eV and for germanium about 0.7 eV.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Small forbidden energy gap allows thermal excitation of electrons at room temperature.

qualitativeClaims.claim: Conductivity of intrinsic semiconductors increases with temperature because more electron-hole pairs are generated thermally.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Higher temperature leads to more carriers crossing the band gap, increasing conductivity (negative temperature coefficient of resistance).

qualitativeClaims.claim: Current in an intrinsic semiconductor is due to both electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Total current = electron current + hole current; both carrier types contribute to conduction.

qualitativeClaims.claim: The Fermi level in an intrinsic semiconductor lies approximately at the middle of the band gap.
qualitativeClaims.expected: EF ≈ (EC + EV)/2 because electron and hole concentrations are equal.

source.question: Explain what an intrinsic semiconductor is.
